new_statements.quote: Toch verdient dit dialect onze aandacht. Hoewel het globaal vrij sterk overeenkomt met het Maleis, heeft het een schat van eigen woorden. Het kenmerkt zich door een zeer rijk gebruik van prae- en suffixen, ook in het gewone spraakgebruik. Door een sterke neiging tot assimilatie, en de zucht om de beginmedeklinker af te werpen, klinkt het zeer vloeiend. Het kent geen e-lemah of zgn. pepet, welke alle worden tot een a en heeft daarbij een duidelijk accent op de paenultima.
new_statements.translation: Still, this dialect deserves our attention. Although on the whole it agrees fairly closely with Malay, it has a wealth of words of its own. It is characterised by a very rich use of prefixes and suffixes, also in ordinary speech. Through a strong tendency to assimilation and the urge to drop the initial consonant, it sounds very fluent. It has no weak e or so-called pepet [schwa], all of which become a, and with that it has a clear accent on the penultimate.
new_statements.citation: Dunselman, P. Donatus. 1949. Bijdrage tot de kennis van de taal en adat der Kendajan Dajaks van West-Borneo [I]. Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 105(1): 59-105. doi:10.1163/22134379-90002488
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (47 pp., Brill open-access BKI 105, downloaded via the Internet Archive) opened; extracted text of PDF p. 3 carries running head '..61' and the Inleiding paragraph exactly as quoted: 'Toch verdient dit dialect onze aandacht.. Het kent geen e-lemah of zgn. pepet, welke alle worden tot een a en heeft daarbij een duidelijk accent op de paenultima.' (text layer lines 103-110 of the. only line-wrap differences). The sentence continues with final-consonant preploded nasals and frequent final hamza, i.e. a genuine (if one-paragraph, impressionistic) phonological characterisation by the fieldworker himself, not second-hand. Reading fixed: penultimate syllable is the only fair reading: a 'clear…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls clearly on the penultimate syllable; the dialect has no schwa (all historical schwas > a), so there is no schwa-conditioned exception of the Malay type.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; the remark is a one-sentence characterisation in an ethnographic-linguistic introduction, not a phonology section.
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic word-level statement by a missionary fieldworker about the spoken dialect of the Mempawah-hinterland Kendayan (Karangan, Toho', Mandor; texts recorded in the Katja' area near Mendjalin). No discussion of phrase-level prosody or citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: ahea1240 'Ahe' is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid for the retired ISO code [ahe], merged in 2008 (CR 2007-261) into Kendayan [knx]; the language-level Glottolog entry is kend1254 (Kendayan/Kanayatn incl. Salako, Belangin). Ahe is the Kanayatn dialect named after its word ahe 'what', spoken in Kab. Landak, Mempawah, Kubu Raya and Bengkayang (per Junita et al. 2016, Ayuni et al. 2020). Dunselman 1949 does not use the name 'Ahe'; he describes the 'Kendajan' dialect of the Dayaks of the Mempawah hinterland (Karangan, Toho', Mandor; texts from the Katja' area near Mendjalin), which is geographically the Ahe area, and his texts show ahe 'what' (p. 62 'Ahé djapasatnnja?', 'na' ahé lain'), so the quoted statement very likely pertains to Ahe Kanayatn specifically rather than to Salako or Belangin. If the catalog files this under the language-level code, use kend1254 with dialect = Ahe (Mempawah/Menjalin Kendayan).

sources.note: Inleiding p. 61, characterising the Kendayan dialect of the Mempawah hinterland (Karangan, Toho', Mandor; texts from the Katja' area near Mendjalin = today's Ahe Kanayatn area; texts use ahe 'what'): no pepet/schwa (all become a) 'en heeft daarbij een duidelijk accent op de paenultima' -- a clear accent on the penultimate.
